title: APEC finally delivers, just not what we hoped for
author: Mark Beeson
text: |Australia, explained.The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will take place in Shenzhen, China, from 18-19 November (Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images)APEC finally delivers, just not what we hoped forXi, Trump and Putin will meet in Shenzhen while the forum’s Australian architects watch on from the sidelines.Mark Beeson17 November 20264 min read|APEC finally delivers, just not what we hoped forAPEC finally delivers, just not what we hoped forAsia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), which former Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans famously described as four adjectives in search of a noun, may finally be about to meet one of its core objectives. Rather revealingly, however, Australia is unlikely to play a major role.This week’s highly anticipated APEC summit in China is attracting unaccustomed attention because it will be the venue for another instalment of what has long been APEC’s most consequential “deliverable”: leaders’-level meetings.Any organisation that can bring Xi Jinping, this year’s host, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin together has to be taken seriously, even if lesser powers are likely to be ignored and left to make up the numbers. Indeed, the fact that their first-ever trilateral meeting will apparently take place on the sidelines of APEC (Opens in new window) is an indication of the latter’s relative geopolitical insignificance.APEC’s admirers may argue that this sort of great power politicking was never what APEC was supposed to be about, and that its expansive geographical format was meant to provide an inclusive forum for encouraging trade and investment liberalisation. Perhaps so, but for APEC’s Australian architects, the ambitions were rather grander.The prospect of the “great powers” getting together to make deals over the heads of the region’s lesser lights is not how things were supposed to develop.As James Curran (Opens in new window)’s excellent new book, Grand Ambition, makes clear, Paul Keating was from the outset focused on the “big picture” and saw APEC primarily as a vehicle for managing regional tensions. While this goal seems closer to realisation, it is not clear whether Australia will get any credit for this, or benefit from the possible outcome of the talks either.The prospect of the “great powers” getting together to make deals over the heads of the region’s lesser lights is not how things were supposed to develop. Neither Keating nor APEC can be blamed for this, though. Rather, it reflects the inability of multilateral organisations (Opens in new window) like APEC and the United Nations to become more inclusive forums in which a range of hitherto overlooked or ignored voices can be heard.So-called “realists” will no doubt argue that it was ever thus, and that power is the only currency that matters in determining international political, economic and especially strategic outcomes. Perhaps so, but the world currently faces unprecedented threats, like rapidly accelerating environmental breakdown, that can only be addressed by widespread cooperation and collective action. APEC’s primary goal of encouraging greater, less regulated economic integration and development seems anachronistic in this context.One area of potential hope, however, in which APEC’s mainly middle power membership might encourage useful cooperation and action, is in responding to the equally urgent challenge posed by artificial intelligence. Not only is it entirely possible that the AI bubble (Opens in new window) may pop and plunge the region into yet another economic crisis, AI also poses a direct threat to the lives and livelihoods of people across the Asia-Pacific.AI featured in the Gyeongju Declaration (Opens in new window) of APEC’s 2025 summit in South Korea. As is the way with APEC, there is a continuing focus on the possible economic benefits of AI, but there is also a recognition that it is going to have significant and differing impacts on the Asia-Pacific labour force and demand for energy. And yet, APEC has neither the mandate nor the capacity to deal with the sometimes perverse effects of unconstrained economic or technological development.President Trump tours the Hall of Prayer of Good Harvest with President Xi in Beijing on 14 May 2026 (Daniel Torok/White House)However, the very act of providing a forum in which Xi and Trump can meet and discuss AI (Opens in new window) in particular is potentially invaluable. After all, it is the relentless competition (Opens in new window) between the world’s superpowers for technological leadership that threatens the strategic status quo and even the presumed deterrent effect (Opens in new window) of nuclear weapons.The chances of coming to agreement over the future course of AI development may not be good given the stakes and the lack of trust, but they are better than the chances of developing a common understanding on the need for action on climate change. On climate, Xi has an incomparably better record (Opens in new window) than Trump, and the coming APEC summit provides an opportunity to remind the world what enlightened environmental leadership looks like.We might hope that middle powers like Australia would take the opportunity to encourage the great powers to think about the general interest rather than just their own. To judge by Australia’s leadership (Opens in new window) at the COP31 climate talks now underway in Antalya, however, there is next to no chance of that.APEC reminds us that it’s one thing to organise an international forum; it’s quite another to generate transformative outcomes that make a difference to people’s lives, whether they live in democracies or autocracies. Whatever you may think about Paul Keating, at least he had grand ambitions.It is testimony to how much has changed since APEC was founded that China, not an original member, may be the best hope of making progress on complex issues that necessitate international cooperation. Xi also has grand ambitions. We must hope he uses the summit to put the collective interest ahead of the national variety.
